p.s: I 'm from a coutry in which history is more than millenary, and it is absolutely true and right that 's always useful and needed to learn from the past to look up to the future, but in my personal life and experience I 've always found that the fact itself ca n't stick permanently in to our memory ( but this may be because I 'm not a huge fan of history too! ), more often it 's the exact contrary, we kind of filter what the fact was trough our senses and what most has captured our attention on the matter.
If nothing has captured our attention it 's more than probable that we wo n't remember it for as much time as needed for the growth of a critical mind.

I 've often been in the situation of having to choose between formation and information ( where for information I mean thetwo or three pointers that can help me in a short time, but wo n't leave me nothing for the future ).

Well, I 've attended classical studies in high school and one of my professors, who has been a real menthor for most of our class, used to say that school has the primary objective to form people, not to inform them, and it can be done only by giving the instruments and possibility to approach a new fact with a proper critical sense.
In other words the students deserve to think with their own minds, preferably open minds.

It has to be assured to them the possibility to dig under the fact, understand it 's logic, by analyzing it from different points of view, discuss it, in a certain sense make it of proper own, infer the essential contents andthen desume a lesson for the future.
